title: Catching a Contradictory-Output Conflict Across Isolated Parallel Agents
description: Tests the ability to distinguish what isolation guarantees from what it doesn't, correctly trace a coordination failure to the decomposition layer rather than either individual agent, and choose human-in-the-loop resolution over a blind rollback-and-retry.

scenario.background: A platform team migrates an internal service's error-response format to a consistent structured schema, split across payments, notifications, and auth modules. A coordinator decomposes the migration into three parallel subtasks, each dispatched to its own coding-agent session on its own branch, in its own isolated ephemeral environment.

characters.name: Wei Zhang
characters.concern: Runs a parallel-output check in addition to the merge check, and catches something the merge tool alone couldn't.

characters.name: Fatima Al-Rashid
characters.concern: Wants the fix traced to its real cause before anything is rolled back or re-run.

questions.stem: The payments and notifications sessions both merge cleanly with no overlapping lines, but standardize the same missing-record error pattern differently — one returns a null/found-false structure, the other throws a NotFoundError. Why didn't the merge-conflict check catch this?
options: Because a merge-conflict check only detects overlapping line-level changes, not whether two independently-produced outputs are semantically compatible with each other
Because the merge tool was misconfigured for this specific repository
Because payments and notifications were never actually run in isolation
Because a merge-conflict check and a parallel-output check are the same thing, so this shouldn't be possible
questions.explanation: A is correct because a merge-conflict check only looks for overlapping line-level edits — it has no concept of whether two changes that don't overlap are still logically or semantically incompatible with each other, which is exactly the gap a contradictory-output conflict falls into: clean on every mechanical check, incompatible in practice. B invents an unsupported explanation. C contradicts the scenario, which explicitly describes isolated environments and separate branches. D conflates two genuinely different checks — this scenario is precisely the case that shows they are not the same thing.

questions.stem: Where does Fatima's team correctly trace the root cause of the contradictory outputs?
options: To a reasoning error inside the payments session specifically
To a reasoning error inside the notifications session specifically

To the coordinator's decomposition: the subtask description told each session *what* to standardize but never specified the *target shape* to standardize to, so each session made a locally reasonable but independently different choice given genuinely incomplete instructions
To a random, unexplainable divergence with no traceable cause
questions.explanation: C is correct because the actual gap is at the decomposition layer — the coordinator never specified a target shape, so each session's choice was locally reasonable given what it was told, not a reasoning failure in either individual session. A and B both misattribute a workflow-level omission to an individual agent that behaved reasonably given its incomplete instructions. D dismisses a fully traceable cause as unexplainable, when the decision record clearly shows the gap.

questions.stem: The auth session hasn't finished yet when the conflict is discovered. What is the correct response?
options: Let the auth session finish and lock in its own independent guess before addressing anything

Pause the auth session before it locks in a third independent guess, have a human resolve the target shape directly, and update the coordinator's subtask template to include that shape explicitly for all three modules
Immediately terminate all three sessions and start the entire migration over from scratch
Ignore the auth session entirely and only fix payments and notifications
questions.explanation: B is correct because pausing the still-running session prevents a third independently-guessed shape from compounding the same ambiguity, and resolving the target shape with a human decision — then fixing the coordinator's template so the ambiguity doesn't recur — addresses the problem at the layer it actually originated from. A lets a third guess lock in before the ambiguity is even resolved. C is a wasteful overcorrection when only the decomposition instructions need fixing, not the entire migration approach. D leaves the auth module's error-format decision unresolved and eventually facing the same gap.

questions.stem: Why is rolling back and simply re-running payments and notifications alone, without changing anything else, not a sufficient fix?
options: Because rollback is never appropriate in a multi-agent system

Because retried against the same underlying, still-ambiguous coordinator instructions, the same ambiguity would reproduce — the fix has to happen at the decomposition layer before re-running either session makes sense
Because the unrelated refactoring changes bundled into each session's diff should also be discarded, not preserved
Because rollback would erase the audit trail needed to reconstruct what happened
questions.explanation: B is correct because re-running either session against the same, still-underspecified coordinator instructions would reproduce the exact same kind of independently-reasonable-but-divergent choice — the fix has to happen at the decomposition layer (specifying the target shape) before a re-run can actually resolve the conflict. A is an overgeneralization the scenario doesn't support — rollback is used here, just not in isolation from fixing the actual cause. C is incorrect — the scenario specifically preserves the still-valid, unrelated parts of each session's diff rather than discarding them wholesale. D is unsupported — the audit artifact recording the decision and rollback is explicitly preserved.

keyLearnings: Isolation (separate branches, separate environments) prevents sessions from interfering with each other, but it does not guarantee their independently-produced outputs are semantically compatible — that requires a separate parallel-output check.

A contradictory-output conflict across independently-reasoning agents often traces to an omission at the decomposition layer (an unspecified target shape), not a reasoning error in any individual agent.
A still-running session should be paused before it locks in its own independent guess once an ambiguity affecting it has been discovered elsewhere.

Rolling back and re-running against the same underspecified instructions reproduces the same failure — the decomposition-layer fix must happen first, and still-valid unrelated work should be preserved rather than discarded wholesale.
